h1:
Ayutthaya Thai Desserts
Thong Yip, Thong Yot, Foi Thong & the Best Shops
intro: Ayutthaya is where a lot of Thailand's royal-court sweets were born. Thong yip, thong yot, foi thong and met khanun all trace back to the palace kitchens of the old Siamese capital, where Thao Thong Kip Ma brought in recipes built on egg yolk and sugar centuries ago. Today you can still find these sweets fresh without much trouble, whether you're walking a market or driving around the old island. We picked the shops and desserts that locals here actually eat and actually buy to take home.
chips: 🪙 Thong yip · thong yot · foi thong

blocks.html: When people think of the golden "thong" sweets, Phetchaburi often comes to mind first, but Ayutthaya is where this family of desserts started. Thao Thong Kip Ma (Marie Guimar) brought Portuguese egg-based sweet recipes into the royal court during King Narai's reign, then adapted them into thong yip, thong yot, foi thong and met khanun, all built around egg yolk and syrup. Today the old capital still has it all, from grandmother-run shops in the villages to a Michelin-recognised mor gaeng custard shop and a new wave of Thai-dessert cafes, so you can pick by your style.

blocks.text: The golden sweets — thong yip, thong yot, foi thong

blocks.html: These three are the stars of any Ayutthaya dessert run. They share the same base of egg yolk and sugar, but the way each shop drops, folds and threads them makes no two the same. The trick is balanced sweetness and an egg aroma that isn't fishy.

items.name: Khanom Thai Pa Mali (Ko Rian)
items.blurb: A grandmother-run, handmade shop in the Ko Rian community making thong yot, foi thong and met khanun that follow the old Thao Thong Kip Ma recipes. The sweets are fresh, with a homey kind of sweetness that doesn't turn sharp. It's a shop that several outlets have visited when tracing original royal-court sweets.

items.name: Khanom Mor Gaeng Mae Yai (Chedi Nakleng / Phai Ling)
items.blurb: One of the first shops locals name when you ask about Ayutthaya sweets, and a Michelin awardee. Beyond the egg, mung-bean and taro custards that are its headline, it also does the full set of thong yip, thong yot and foi thong. Sit down in the cool air-conditioned shop or grab a box to take home.
items.meta: Phai Ling subdistrict · open 08:00–19:00 · from 40–60 THB

items.name: Baan Khao Nom (U Thong Road, old island)
items.blurb: A Thai-dessert cafe in the old town with a cute retro Thai look. It serves the golden sweets along with other Thai desserts and drinks, so it's a good spot to rest after temple-hopping and pick up something to take home too.
items.meta: U Thong Road, old island · around 101–250 THB per person

items.name: Thai dessert stalls at Chao Phrom Market
items.blurb: The main market for Ayutthaya locals, along Naresuan Road, with several Thai-sweet stalls selling thong yot, foi thong, khanom chan and khanom piakpoon at easy prices. Great for grabbing a bunch of different sweets in one place before you head out.
items.meta: Chao Phrom Market, Naresuan Road · market-stall prices

blocks.title: Tips for buying
blocks.html: The golden sweets are made from egg yolk, so they don't keep as long as dry-baked goods. If you're carrying them far, buy them on your day of travel and tell the seller how many more hours you'll be on the road. Many shops will box and split-pack them to suit the distance.

blocks.text: Mor gaeng custard and other Old Capital sweets

blocks.html: Beyond the golden sweets, Ayutthaya is also known for dense, coconut-scented mor gaeng custard and for roti sai mai, which has basically become the province's signature souvenir. These two are the most popular things to carry home alongside the golden sweets.

items.name: Mor gaeng custard (Old Capital style)
items.blurb: Custard made with egg, mung bean, taro or lotus seed, dense with a fragrant browned top and a sweetness that doesn't go sharp. It's a dessert Ayutthaya does in a soft, deep way. You can find it at Mae Yai and at stalls in Chao Phrom Market.

items.name: Roti sai mai (Abidin / Mae Pom)
items.blurb: Ayutthaya's signature souvenir: a thin sheet of roti wrapped around spun sugar that pulls into silky sweet threads. Well-known makers like Abidin and Mae Pom have been at it for ages, and they're easy to find near the hospital and around the old island.
items.meta: around the old island · 20–30 THB per set

items.name: Hom Klin Thai Dessert Cafe (Wat Ratchaburana view)
items.blurb: A newer Thai-dessert cafe with a view over Wat Ratchaburana. It has Thai sweets, light savoury bites and drinks, good for photos and a break between temple visits. The sweets are packed nicely enough to carry home as gifts.
items.meta: near Wat Ratchaburana, old island · cafe

items.name: Chu Jai Dessert
items.blurb: A shaved-ice and dessert-buffet style shop with easy prices, around 35–40 THB a bowl. Good for cooling off after walking temples in the heat, with plenty of Thai sweets to choose from in one place.
items.meta: in Ayutthaya town · about 35–40 THB per bowl

items.name: Cake Baan Suan (Wang Noi)
items.blurb: A souvenir from Wang Noi district: soft cakes with a range of fillings at fair prices. People regularly stop for them on the way in and out of Ayutthaya on the Wang Noi side. Not a royal-court sweet, but a popular take-home that pairs well with the rest.

blocks.text: How to buy Thai desserts as souvenirs and get your money's worth

items: Sort by travel distance — egg sweets (thong yip, thong yot, foi thong) keep for 2–3 days · mor gaeng keeps longer chilled · roti sai mai keeps dry for several days.
Buy from shops that make it daily — the golden sweets taste best fresh, so if you can see them being made out front, or they tell you it was made this morning, you're on safer ground.
Stock up on variety at Chao Phrom Market — if you want several kinds on a budget, one loop through Chao Phrom Market does it.
Ask about the sweetness — many shops make two levels, so tell the seller if you prefer it less sweet. A good royal-court sweet is rounded, not sharp.

items.name: Temple-hopping + desserts
items.blurb: Walk the temples on the old island in the morning, then stop at Baan Khao Nom or Hom Klin for Thai sweets in the afternoon.

items.name: Serious souvenir run
items.blurb: Drive over to Mae Yai for mor gaeng and golden sweets, then grab roti sai mai around the old island before you leave.

faq.q: Do thong yip, thong yot and foi thong really come from Ayutthaya?
faq.a: The golden sweets trace back to the Ayutthaya royal court during King Narai's reign, when Thao Thong Kip Ma brought in Portuguese egg-based sweet recipes and adapted them into thong yip, thong yot, foi thong and met khanun. You can still find them today both in the Ko Rian community and at Thai-dessert shops around the old island.

faq.q: Where's the best place to buy Thai desserts as souvenirs in Ayutthaya?
faq.a: If you want everything in one place, try Khanom Mor Gaeng Mae Yai or Chao Phrom Market. For handmade, original-recipe sweets, try Khanom Thai Pa Mali in Ko Rian, and don't forget roti sai mai from a well-known maker, which is the province's signature souvenir.

faq.q: How long do the golden sweets keep?
faq.a: Because they're made from egg yolk and syrup, thong yip, thong yot and foi thong are best eaten within 2–3 days and kept cool. If you're travelling far, buy them on your day of departure and tell the seller how many more hours you'll be on the road so they can pack them to suit the distance.

faq.q: How many branches does Khanom Mor Gaeng Mae Yai have, and what are the prices?
faq.a: Khanom Mor Gaeng Mae Yai has several branches in Ayutthaya, such as Chedi Nakleng and Phai Ling, open roughly 08:00–19:00. Sweets start at around 40–60 THB, and its Michelin recognition vouches for that traditional flavour.

faq.q: Where can I eat Thai desserts in a cafe setting?
faq.a: Try Baan Khao Nom on U Thong Road on the old island, decorated in a retro Thai style, or Hom Klin, a Thai-dessert cafe with a view over Wat Ratchaburana. Both have a range of Thai sweets to choose from and can pack them to take home.
